profile.feeling: Basic and everyday; in figurative use, something that slowly destroys.

senses.def: to eat away, corrode, consume (rust, fire, time)

examples.tr: What do you eat for breakfast?

phrases.tr: time has eaten and drunk on it
phrases.meaning: it is very old, worn out or outdated

synonyms.nuance: to have, take (a meal, medicine) — news, menus and polite speech
to devour, gobble up

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔakal-; cognate with Hebrew אָכַל (akhal) and Aramaic ʾăḵal.

funFacts: The imperative is just كُلْ (kul, ‘eat!’): like خُذْ (‘take!’) and مُرْ (‘order!’) it drops its first radical, the hamza.
pitfalls: I eat = آكُلُ (ʾākulu): hamza + long ā is written with madda, آ.
The vowel of the 2nd radical changes: a in the past (أَكَلَ), u in the present (يَأْكُلُ).
subtleties: In formal Arabic, especially for meals, تَنَاوَلَ is preferred: تَنَاوَلْنَا الْغَدَاءَ (we had lunch).

profile.feeling: Everyday and social: tea, coffee, hospitality.

examples.tr: What will you (f) have to drink?
My grandfather smokes shisha at the café.

phrases.meaning: do what you like, I don’t care (a rude dismissal)

synonyms.nuance: to have, take (food, drink, medicine) — polite and written style
to sip, drink slowly (a hot drink)

etymology.text: Root ش ر ب; compare Akkadian sarāpum (“to suck”) and Geʿez ሠረበ (śäräbä).

funFacts: English syrup and sherbet, Turkish şerbet and Greek σιρόπι all come from this root: شَرَاب / شَرْبَة, “a drink”.
pitfalls: The vowel changes: šariba (past, i) → yašrabu (present, a). Not *yašribu.
شَرَّبَ with šadda is a different verb: “to make drink, to soak” (form II).
subtleties: In formal or polite language تَنَاوَلَ is preferred for meals and medicine: تَنَاوَلَ الدَّوَاءَ.

profile.feeling: Home, family kitchens and the smell of a pot on the stove.

examples.tr: My mother cooks rice every day.

collocations.tr: to cook on a low heat

synonyms.nuance: to cook — formal and written style; the cook / chef is طَاهٍ

etymology.text: From the root ط ب خ (ṭ b ḫ). Cognate with Hebrew טבח (tavákh, “to slaughter, to butcher”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The root gives مَطْبَخ (kitchen, the place pattern mafʿal) and طَبَّاخ (cook, the trade pattern faʿʿāl); Turkish mutfak, “kitchen”, is the Arabic مَطْبَخ.
In Hebrew the same root means “to slaughter”, but Modern Hebrew טַבָּח (tabach) is “a cook” — the butcher and the cook meet in one word.
pitfalls: The present has u: يَطْبُخُ (yaṭbuḫu), أَطْبُخُ — not *yaṭbaḫu.
خ (ḫ, the ch of German Bach) is not ح (ḥ): ṭabaḫa.
subtleties: The dish is a direct object, no preposition: أَطْبُخُ السَّمَكَ (I cook fish).
Menus and recipes also use the formal طَهَا / طَهْو; at home people say طَبَخَ.

profile.feeling: Wishes and intentions; direct, so softened with مِنْ فَضْلِكَ.

examples.text: أُرِيدُ كُوبًا مِنَ الْمَاءِ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ.
examples.tr: I would like a glass of water, please.
What do you (f) want to eat?
They want to travel to Morocco.

examples.text: فَوَجَدَا فِيهَا جِدَارًا يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَنْقَضَّ
examples.tr: and they found in it a wall about to collapse (Qurʾān 18:77)

phrases.text: إِذَا أَرَدْتَ أَنْ تُطَاعَ فَأْمُرْ بِمَا يُسْتَطَاعُ
phrases.tr: if you want to be obeyed, order what can be done
phrases.meaning: make demands that people are able to meet

synonyms.nuance: to wish, would like — very polite: أَوَدُّ أَنْ أَشْكُرَكُمْ (I would like to thank you)
to desire, wish for — written and official style

etymology.text: Form IV of the root ر و د; verbal noun إِرَادَة, “will, intention” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish irade (will, decree) and mürit (disciple) come from Arabic إِرَادَة and مُرِيد, “one who wants”, from this root.
pitfalls: Hollow verb: the long ī/ā shortens before consonant endings — تُرِيدُ but تُرِدْنَ (you, women, want); أَرَادَ but أَرَدْتُ (I wanted).
Form IV: present with u-prefix — أُرِيدُ, يُرِيدُ (not *أَرِيدُ).
subtleties: Followed by a noun (أُرِيدُ خُبْزًا) or by أَنْ + subjunctive (أُرِيدُ أَنْ آكُلَ). In a shop, أُرِيدُ + مِنْ فَضْلِكَ is fine; أَوَدُّ is more formal.

profile.feeling: Warm; from “I like onions” to “I love you”.

examples.tr: Do you like tea with mint?

collocations.tr: to love with all one’s heart

phrases.text: مَنْ أَحَبَّ شَيْئًا أَكْثَرَ مِنْ ذِكْرِهِ
phrases.tr: whoever loves a thing mentions it often
phrases.meaning: people keep talking about what they love

synonyms.nuance: to love passionately, be infatuated
to love, be fond of — classical and poetic
“to please”: أَعْجَبَنِي الْفِيلْمُ = I liked the film — the thing liked is the subject

etymology.text: Form IV of the root ح ب ب; the verbal nouns are حُبّ (love) and مَحَبَّة (affection) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish muhabbet (friendly chat, affection) comes from Arabic مَحَبَّة, from the same root; Hebrew חִבָּה (ḥiba, fondness) is a Semitic cousin.
pitfalls: Form IV: the present has u-prefixes — أُحِبُّ (ʾuḥibbu), يُحِبُّ — not *أَحِبُّ.
Doubled root: before a consonant ending the two b’s come apart — أَحْبَبْتُ (I loved), يُحْبِبْنَ (they, women, love).
subtleties: أُحِبُّ means both “I like” and “I love”; the object decides: أُحِبُّ الْبَصَلَ (I like onions) vs أُحِبُّكِ (I love you).
To like doing: أُحِبُّ + verbal noun (أُحِبُّ السِّبَاحَةَ) or أَنْ + subjunctive (أُحِبُّ أَنْ أَسْبَحَ).

profile.feeling: Markets, shopping, bargaining.

examples.tr: I bought bread at the bakery.
What are you buying for dinner?

examples.text: نَشْتَرِي الْخُضَارَ مِنَ السُّوقِ كُلَّ أُسْبُوعٍ.
examples.tr: We buy vegetables at the market every week.
My sister bought a new dress.

synonyms.nuance: to buy, purchase — written and formal style
classical form I: can mean “to buy” but also “to sell” (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Form VIII (pattern اِفْتَعَلَ) of the root ش ر ي, whose form I شَرَى can mean both “to sell” and “to buy” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: مُشْتَرٍ means “buyer” — and الْمُشْتَرِي is also the planet Jupiter.
pitfalls: Weak final radical: the y appears as -ā, -ī or -ay — اِشْتَرَى (he bought), يَشْتَرِي (he buys), اِشْتَرَيْتُ (I bought), اِشْتَرَوْا (they bought).
تَشْتَرِينَ is both “you (one woman) buy” and “you (women) buy”.
subtleties: The initial alif is a connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl): after a vowel it is silent — وَاشْتَرَى (wa-štarā).

profile.feeling: The staple of every Arab table: flat bread, warm from the bakery.

examples.tr: We eat bread with every meal.
I bought fresh bread at the bakery.

phrases.tr: there is bread and salt between us
phrases.meaning: we have eaten together — a bond of loyalty that must not be betrayed

synonyms.nuance: bread in Egyptian Arabic — literally “life”

etymology.text: Wiktionary: often suspected to be a loan (an Aksumite or Old South Arabian forerunner of Geʿez ḫəbəst), the root خ ب ز being derived secondarily from خُبْزَة “a loaf”; or, both via Old Aramaic, from Old Georgian ჴუეზაჲ (quezay, “loaf of bread”).

funFacts: The same root gives خَبَزَ (to bake), مَخْبَز (bakery, the place pattern mafʿal) and خَبَّاز (baker).
pitfalls: A mass noun: “a loaf” is رَغِيفُ خُبْزٍ (or خُبْزَة), not *خُبْزٌ وَاحِدٌ.
subtleties: Bread in general takes the article: أُحِبُّ الْخُبْزَ = I like bread; خُبْزًا (indefinite) = some bread: أَشْتَرِي خُبْزًا.

profile.feeling: Breakfast tables: white cheese, olives and bread.

synonyms.nuance: a cheese, a piece of cheese; in Levantine and Egyptian speech the usual word for cheese

etymology.text: From the root ج ب ن (j b n). Compare Hebrew גְּבִינָה (g’viná, “cheese”) and Classical Syriac ܓܒܬܐ (gḇettā, “cheese, curd”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew גְּבִינָה (gvina) is the same Semitic word.
pitfalls: Same letters and vowels as جُبْن “cowardice” (from جَبُنَ, “to be cowardly”; جَبَان = coward) — only the context tells them apart.
subtleties: A mass noun: cheese as food is جُبْن; one cheese or a piece is جُبْنَة.

profile.feeling: Breakfast: boiled or fried eggs.

examples.tr: I eat two eggs every morning.

phrases.text: لَا تَضَعْ كُلَّ الْبَيْضِ فِي سَلَّةٍ وَاحِدَةٍ
phrases.tr: don’t put all the eggs in one basket
phrases.meaning: don’t risk everything on one thing

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: بَيْض is the word in Standard Arabic and in the dialects.

etymology.text: Cognate with Hebrew בֵּיצָה (bēṣā) and Classical Syriac ܒܝܥܬܐ (bēʿṯā) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The root ب ي ض also gives أَبْيَض, “white”.
Hebrew בֵּיצָה (beytsa), “egg”, is the same word.
pitfalls: بَيْض = eggs (as food, in general), بَيْضَة = one egg, بَيْضَتَانِ = two eggs, ثَلَاثُ بَيْضَاتٍ = three eggs.
subtleties: A collective is masculine singular for agreement: الْبَيْضُ طَازَجٌ (the eggs are fresh).

profile.feeling: Feasts and grills; for some families an everyday food, for others a treat.

examples.tr: My father bought meat for dinner.

phrases.tr: the flesh is yours and the bones are ours
phrases.meaning: old words of parents handing a child to a teacher: be strict with him, only bring him back whole

profile.synonymsNone: No neutral synonym; kinds of meat are named لَحْمُ + the animal (لَحْمُ بَقَرٍ, beef).

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *laḥm- (“food, eatables; meat, bread”); cognate with Aramaic laḥmā, Hebrew לֶחֶם (léḥem), Ugaritic lḥm, Geʿez lahm, all meaning “food” or “bread” — the senses split with the different diets of Arabia and the Fertile Crescent (Wiktionary).

funFacts: One Semitic word, two foods: Arabic لَحْم is “meat”, Hebrew לֶחֶם is “bread”. Bethlehem is Hebrew “house of bread” — and in Arabic بَيْتُ لَحْمٍ, “house of meat”.
pitfalls: ل is a sun letter: the article is written with šadda — اللَّحْمُ (al-laḥmu).
subtleties: Meat in general takes the article (أُحِبُّ اللَّحْمَ); the plural لُحُوم means kinds of meat (in shops and on menus).

profile.feeling: The coast and the market: grilled fish by the sea.

senses.def: fish (as food and in general); سَمَكَة = one fish

examples.tr: There are many fish in the sea.

synonyms.nuance: in the Qurʾān a (big) fish — Jonah’s; in Modern Standard Arabic “whale”

etymology.text: From the root س م ك (s m k), “to be elevated, to be held up, to sustain” — hence “a source of sustenance, a staple food”; cognate with Hebrew סָמַךְ (samakh, “to lean, support”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: If Wiktionary’s etymology is right, fish was named as “what sustains you” — the Hebrew relative סָמַךְ means “to support”.
pitfalls: سَمَك = fish as food or fish in general; one fish = سَمَكَة; أَسْمَاك = (many / kinds of) fish. The counting plural سَمَكَات (ثَلَاثُ سَمَكَاتٍ) is also used.
أَسْمَاك is a non-human plural: feminine singular agreement — أَسْمَاكٌ كَثِيرَةٌ.
subtleties: Two fish: سَمَكَتَانِ (the dual of the unit noun).

profile.feeling: Grilled chicken with rice — the everyday feast.

examples.tr: We cook the chicken with rice.
This hen lays an egg every day.

phrases.tr: which came first: the chicken or the egg?
phrases.meaning: a question with no clear answer

synonyms.nuance: a (young) chicken, especially grilled — Levantine and Iraqi usage

etymology.text: Wiktionary: unknown, probably onomatopoeic — compare دِجْ دِجْ (dij dij), the call for chickens, and دَجْدَجَ, “to call a chicken”.

funFacts: A rooster is a different word: دِيك.
pitfalls: Food: الدَّجَاجُ (collective); one bird: دَجَاجَةٌ (a hen, a chicken); two: دَجَاجَتَانِ.
subtleties: Wiktionary also gives the pronunciation dijāj (دِجَاج).

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses أَرُزّ as “alternative form of رُزّ (ruzz)”, and رُزّ means “rice”; أَرُزّ is the Standard Arabic form.

profile.feeling: The base of many dishes: rice with chicken, rice with vegetables.

senses.def: rice (the grain and the cooked food)

examples.tr: My mother cooks rice with vegetables.
I’d like a plate of rice, please.

synonyms.nuance: the other common form (ruzz) — Wiktionary’s main entry; usual in many dialects

etymology.text: Wiktionary: an alternative form of رُزّ (ruzz), borrowed from Aramaic ʔăruzzā / ʔuruzzā; the etymology tree goes back through Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óruza) to an Iranian word.

funFacts: A Greek word in Arabic: ὄρυζα → Aramaic → Arabic الرُّزّ, which gave Spanish and Portuguese arroz.
pitfalls: Not أَرْز (ʾarz): that is the cedar, the tree on Lebanon’s flag.
subtleties: A mass noun: one grain is حَبَّةُ أَرُزٍّ; dishes are named by what is in them: أَرُزٌّ بِالدَّجَاجِ.

profile.feeling: Winter evenings and Ramadan tables: a bowl of lentil soup.

examples.text: تَطْبُخُ أُمِّي حَسَاءَ الْعَدَسِ فِي الشِّتَاءِ.
examples.tr: My mother cooks lentil soup in winter.
I have soup when I’m ill.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word for soup in most Arab countries and on menus — the same word as Turkish çorba (from Persian)

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology section; the word belongs to the root ح س و of حَسَا, “to sip”: soup is “what is sipped”.

funFacts: Soup is drunk, not eaten, in Arabic: نَشْرَبُ الْحَسَاءَ.
pitfalls: It ends in hamza after ā: the indefinite accusative is حَسَاءً, with no extra alif.
subtleties: In speech and on most menus you will read شُورْبَة; حَسَاء is the Standard Arabic word of books and the news.

profile.feeling: Fresh and colourful: the salad that comes with every meal.
profile.synonymsNone: The only common word; kinds of salad are named after what is in them (سَلَطَةُ خُضَارٍ).

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology; it is a European loanword, the Italian (in)salata (“salted”) that Greek σαλάτα and Turkish salata also borrowed.

funFacts: One dish, one word around the Mediterranean: Arabic سَلَطَة, Greek σαλάτα, Turkish salata, Italian insalata.
pitfalls: Unvocalized سلطة is also سُلْطَة (sulṭa), “power, authority” (plural سُلُطَات) — read the vowels.
subtleties: س is a sun letter: السَّلَطَةُ (as-salaṭa).

profile.feeling: Markets full of colour: oranges, grapes, figs and dates.

examples.tr: The banana is a tasty fruit.
There are lots of fruits at the market.

synonyms.nuance: the fruit of any plant, also figurative “result”; فَاكِهَة is fruit as food

etymology.text: A word of the root ف ك ه (Wiktionary); Wiktionary’s entry has no etymology section.

funFacts: Fruit and fun share a root: فُكَاهَة means “humour, a joke” and فَكِه “cheerful”.
pitfalls: The plural فَوَاكِهُ is a diptote: no tanwīn — فَوَاكِهُ, and فَوَاكِهَ for both accusative and genitive.
subtleties: The singular also means fruit in general: أُحِبُّ الْفَاكِهَةَ (I like fruit); فَوَاكِه stresses several kinds.

profile.feeling: Crunchy and everyday; red, green and yellow at the greengrocer’s.

examples.tr: I eat an apple every day.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: according to Fraenkel a borrowing from Aramaic (the etymon is not clearly attested there); compare Hebrew תַּפּוּחַ (tappūaḥ), Ugaritic tpḥ and Punic *tappūḥ.

funFacts: Hebrew תַּפּוּחַ (tapuach) is the same word — and Hebrew “potato” is תַּפּוּחַ אֲדָמָה, “apple of the earth”, like French pomme de terre.
pitfalls: التُّفَّاحُ = apples (in general), تُفَّاحَةٌ = one apple, ثَلَاثُ تُفَّاحَاتٍ = three apples.
subtleties: ت is a sun letter: التُّفَّاحُ (at-tuffāḥ).

profile.feeling: Sweet tea and sweet coffee: “how much sugar?” is a real question.

examples.tr: Do you want sugar in your coffee?

etymology.text: Borrowed from Middle Persian šakar, from Gandhari śakara, from Sanskrit शर्करा (śárkarā), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorkeh₂ (“gravel”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English sugar, German Zucker and Spanish azúcar came to Europe through Arabic سُكَّر; Greek ζάχαρη and Russian сахар are cousins from the same Sanskrit word.
pitfalls: Double k (šadda): سُكَّر (sukkar). سُكْر (sukr) is “drunkenness” and سَكَر (sakar) “an intoxicant” (Wiktionary).
subtleties: In everyday talk سُكَّر also means diabetes; the medical word is السُّكَّرِيّ.

profile.feeling: Salt on the table — and the old bond of “bread and salt”.

examples.tr: Don’t put in too much salt.

phrases.tr: there is bread and salt between us
phrases.meaning: we have eaten together — a bond of loyalty that must not be betrayed

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-West Semitic *milḥ- (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Same root: مَالِح (salty) and مَلَّاح (sailor). Hebrew מֶלַח (melach) is the same word — the Dead Sea is יָם הַמֶּלַח, “the Sea of Salt”.
pitfalls: ح (ḥ), not خ or ه: milḥ — and the vowel is i: مِلْح, not *مَلْح.
subtleties: A mass noun: “a pinch of salt” = رَشَّةُ مِلْحٍ.

profile.feeling: Life itself in a hot climate; the first thing offered to a guest.

examples.tr: Drink lots of water in summer.

phrases.text: وَجَعَلْنَا مِنَ الْمَاءِ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ حَيٍّ
phrases.tr: and We made every living thing from water
phrases.meaning: water as the origin of life

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in prose; poetic and dialect forms (مَيّ, mayya) exist.

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *māy-, from Proto-Afroasiatic *maʔ-; the plural was reanalyzed as if from a root م و ه. Cognate with Hebrew מַיִם (máyim) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew מַיִם (mayim) is the same word; in many dialects “water” is mayya.
pitfalls: Accusative indefinite مَاءً — no extra alif after the hamza.
The plural مِيَاه means waters: mineral water, sea water, the water supply.
subtleties: Water is not counted: one glass is كَأْسُ مَاءٍ.

profile.feeling: Hospitality in a small glass: sweet tea, often with mint.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Persian چای (čây, “tea”), possibly from Chinese 茶葉 (“tea leaves”); ultimately from Chinese 茶 (chá, “tea”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: One word across your languages: Arabic شَاي, Turkish çay, Russian чай and Greek τσάι all go back to Chinese 茶 (chá).
pitfalls: In many Arab countries tea comes in a small glass: كَأْسُ شَايٍ, not فِنْجَانُ شَايٍ.
subtleties: The final ي is a consonant here: شَايٌ (šāyun), شَايًا, شَايٍ.

profile.feeling: Strong, small and social: cardamom coffee for guests.

senses.def: café, coffee house (Egyptian and other dialects; Standard مَقْهًى)

examples.tr: I drink a cup of coffee every morning.
Arabic coffee is a symbol of hospitality.

examples.text: يَجْلِسُ جَدِّي فِي الْقَهْوَةِ مَعَ أَصْدِقَائِهِ.
examples.tr: My grandfather sits in the café with his friends.

synonyms.nuance: coffee beans, ground coffee — not the drink

etymology.text: Wiktionary: medieval philologists derived it from the root ق ه ي (relating to satiety) with the meaning “wine”; the word for a brew, first mulled wine, later passed to coffee. The ultimate origin is disputed.

funFacts: Coffee, German Kaffee, Turkish kahve, Greek καφές and Russian кофе all go back to Arabic قَهْوَة (through Ottoman Turkish kahve).
pitfalls: Feminine: الْقَهْوَةُ سَاخِنَةٌ (the coffee is hot), not *سَاخِنٌ.
subtleties: In Egypt قَهْوَة is also the café; Standard Arabic says مَقْهًى (the place pattern mafʿal).

profile.feeling: Children’s breakfasts and milky tea.

examples.tr: The child drinks milk before bed.
I drink my coffee with milk.
We bought a litre of milk.

synonyms.nuance: milk in Classical Arabic and in Egypt; in the Levant and the Gulf it means yogurt or buttermilk

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥalīb- (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew חָלָב (chalav), “milk”, is the same word; the Arabic verb حَلَبَ means “to milk”.
pitfalls: ح (ḥ), not خ: ḥalīb.
subtleties: Which word for milk you hear depends on the country: حَلِيب is understood everywhere and is the Standard word.

profile.feeling: Juice bars and fresh orange juice on a hot day.

synonyms.nuance: a drink, also syrup; عَصِير is pressed from fruit

etymology.text: Nominalized adjective from the root ع ص ر (ʕ ṣ r); compare عَصَرَ (ʕaṣara, “to press, to squeeze”), Classical Syriac ʿəṣārā (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The verb عَصَرَ is “to squeeze”, and مِعْصَرَة (the tool pattern mifʿala) is a press — an olive press, for example.
pitfalls: The plural عَصَائِرُ is a diptote (no tanwīn).
Do not confuse it with عَصْر (ʿaṣr), “afternoon; era”.
subtleties: “Juice of X” = عَصِيرُ + X in the genitive: عَصِيرُ تُفَّاحٍ (apple juice).

profile.feeling: Restaurant menus and travel; a drink many Muslims do not take.

examples.tr: France is famous for its wine.

synonyms.nuance: wine, any intoxicating drink — the Qurʾānic and classical word (feminine)

etymology.text: From the Middle Persian ancestor of Classical Persian نبید (nabīd) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: In early Islamic times نَبِيذ was a drink of dates or raisins steeped in water — fermented only if it was left standing.
pitfalls: Islam forbids alcohol and many people do not drink it: offer juice or tea unless you know your guest.
subtleties: ن is a sun letter: النَّبِيذُ (an-nabīḏ).

profile.feeling: A modern loanword: bars, hotels — and alcohol-free beer.

synonyms.nuance: the Standard Arabic word of dictionaries and official texts; people say بِيرَة

etymology.text: Borrowed from Italian birra, possibly through Greek μπίρα (bíra) or Ottoman Turkish bira; ultimately from German Bier (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A word that crossed your languages: German Bier → Italian birra → (Greek μπίρα or Turkish bira) → Arabic بِيرَة.
pitfalls: Feminine (ة): بِيرَةٌ بَارِدَةٌ, not *بَارِدٌ.
subtleties: A mass noun; “a beer” is زُجَاجَةُ بِيرَةٍ (a bottle) or كَأْسُ بِيرَةٍ (a glass). Wiktionary also notes the spelling بِيرَا.

profile.feeling: Bread, cheese, olives, eggs and tea — the morning table.

examples.tr: I have bread and cheese for breakfast.
Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.

synonyms.nuance: breakfast in formal use (hotels); above all the meal that breaks the fast at sunset in Ramadan

etymology.text: From the root ف ط ر, “to break (a fast)”: Wiktionary lists فَطُور (faṭūr) “breakfast” beside فُطُور (fuṭūr), the verbal noun of فَطَرَ, and إِفْطَار, the verbal noun of أَفْطَرَ.

funFacts: Exactly like English break-fast: the meal that breaks the night’s fast.
pitfalls: faṭūr (فَطُور) is the meal; fuṭūr (فُطُور) is the act of breaking a fast — but in speech you will also hear fuṭūr for breakfast.
subtleties: With meals Arabic says عَلَى: عَلَى الْفَطُورِ (at breakfast); prepositions come in lesson 11.

profile.feeling: The main family meal in many Arab homes, in the early afternoon.

examples.tr: We eat lunch at two o’clock.
My friend invited me to lunch.

profile.synonymsNone: No other Standard Arabic word for lunch.

etymology.text: Wiktionary compares غَدًا (ġadan, “tomorrow”) and غَدَاة (ġadāh, “morning”); it also records the older sense “breakfast”.

funFacts: The word once meant the morning meal (Wiktionary still lists “breakfast”) and moved to midday; the same root gives غَدًا, “tomorrow”.
pitfalls: غَدَاء (lunch, with د) ≠ غِذَاء (food, nourishment, with ذ).
subtleties: Ends in hamza after ā: accusative indefinite غَدَاءً, no extra alif.

profile.feeling: The evening meal: often light at home, festive when guests come.

examples.tr: We invited our friends to dinner.

profile.synonymsNone: No other Standard Arabic word for the evening meal.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the verbal noun of عَشَا (form I), root ع ش و; compare عِشَاء, “dusk, nightfall”.

funFacts: Arabic-speaking Christians call the Last Supper الْعَشَاءُ الْأَخِيرُ.
pitfalls: عَشَاء (ʿašāʾ, dinner) ≠ عِشَاء (ʿišāʾ, nightfall; the night prayer صَلَاةُ الْعِشَاءِ). Unvocalized both are عشاء.
subtleties: Accusative indefinite عَشَاءً — no extra alif after the hamza.
